A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study of transformer sensitivity despite the changed title and conference formatting. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, proofs, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-data, vision, language, corruption-robustness, and sharpness experiments in Sections 4–7 and Appendix A.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds ImageNet comparisons, perturbation analyses, and modular-addition and sparse-parity learning results.

M1.justification: The synthetic self-attention model, token-replacement and Gaussian-perturbation sensitivity procedures, image augmentation, and patch-output MSE regularization are retained. The reorganized sensitivity definition and its application as a training-progress diagnostic do not establish a change to the underlying method.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on ImageNet-1k's broader image-classification population, modular addition modulo 113, and sparse parity with dimension 40 and sparsity 4. The original synthetic, MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, SVHN, MRPC, QQP, and CIFAR-10-C coverage remains, including material moved to the appendices.

E2.justification: v2 adds ConvMixer to the existing CIFAR-10 architecture comparison and evaluates pretrained ConvNext, specified as ConvNextV2-Tiny in Appendix D, against ViT/L-16 on ImageNet. These extend the comparison to a patch-processing control and another pretrained architecture. Figure 8 also evaluates weight norm as an alternative progress diagnostic. Original comparators, including GPT-2 in the appendix, remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include ImageNet sensitivity evaluation on 20,000 training images with variance 15, whole-input noise comparisons, a CIFAR-10 noise-variance sweep, and algorithmic-task training experiments. Sparse-parity experiments vary sample sizes, batch sizes, embedding dimensions, and learning rates. The synthetic alignment vector is corrected from e1−e3 to e1−e2; this is a reported metric correction without evidence that the retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: v2 tests whether patch processing explains low sensitivity using ConvMixer, compares whole-input and token-wise perturbations in Table 4, and examines vision noise strength in Figure 14. Sections 7.3 and A.5–A.6 add training-progress analyses for grokking and sparse parity. The optimizer, depth/head, GPT-2, validation-set, and corruption-severity analyses already present in v1 are retained.

E5.justification: v2 introduces explicit seed-wise reporting for the new algorithmic experiments: Figure 23 plots three grokking seed trajectories, and Appendix A.6 specifies seeds including 0, 42, and 123. This does not establish additional runs for retained experiments. The existing five-noise-repeat estimates remain, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are introduced.

E6.justification: New results include ConvMixer sensitivity of 0.0829 on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet sensitivities of 0.0191 for ViT/L-16 versus 0.0342 for ConvNext. Table 4 adds whole-input-noise results, while Figures 8, 23, and 24 report sensitivity tracking learning progress, including sparse-parity convergence to 0.1. Original synthetic, vision, language, corruption, and sharpness results are largely retained; these additions are not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: v2 adds Proposition 3.2 and its Appendix B.2 proof, bounding Boolean prediction disagreement under correlated noise by (1−rho^(Smax(f)^2))/2 through noise stability and Fourier degree. It also corrects D(f) from an approximation-degree description to the degree of the polynomial representing f. Proposition 3.1 and its spectral-bias proof are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion add sensitivity as a progress measure for grokking and a theoretical connection between low sensitivity and noise robustness. The architecture-comparison claim expands to ConvMixer and pretrained vision models. The original low-sensitivity, robustness-intervention, and flatter-minima claims remain; flatness was already a contribution in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning patch processing, the choice of perturbation metric, and grokking phases, including a proposed Fourier noise-reduction phase. Appendix E newly discusses pretraining-data and optimizer limitations while retaining the unresolved theoretical comparison between architectures. Section 7.1 softens causal language and removes v1's extrapolation from corruption robustness to adversarial robustness; the speculative OOD-feature argument is also removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-code link, implementation and licensing information, GPU specifications and runtimes, and settings for ConvMixer, ImageNet, and sparse-parity experiments. Appendix D newly discloses approximately 30% training-data sampling for vision sensitivity measurement; v1's wording does not establish that this sampling procedure changed. Five patch perturbations and regularization strength 0.25 were already documented in v1.

R1.justification: v2 adds relevant positioning around Hahn and Rofin's Boolean-sensitivity work, Gopalan et al.'s locality discussion, and progress-measure literature including Barak et al. and Chen et al. Most existing related-work discussions and the positioning as an extension beyond Boolean inputs remain. The spectral-bias subsection substantially reorganizes material already discussed in v1.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Sensitivity measurement becomes the organizing topic of Section 4, with synthetic experiments nested beneath it. Kernel background and dataset descriptions move to appendices, and the discussion structure is replaced by a conclusion and separate limitations section.

P2.justification: v2 adopts conference formatting and substantially rearranges displays. The existing final-epoch robustness summary moves into the main text with revised markers and caption, while corruption-training curves and Fashion-MNIST/SVHN plots move to the appendix. The CIFAR-10 display adds ConvMixer and separates overview panels from full dynamics. New displays cover perturbation comparisons, variance sensitivity, grokking, and sparse parity.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central empirical argument: ConvMixer addresses whether patch processing alone explains the effect, perturbation analyses examine dependence on the sensitivity definition, and ImageNet tests extend evidence beyond small vision benchmarks. Seed-wise algorithmic results and added code, sampling, and compute disclosures further improve support and reproducibility. The Boolean bound does not establish comparative robustness between architectures, and the grokking mechanism remains inferential, but these limits do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and clarity.
